items.title: The TCP three-way handshake
items.body: A connection opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, exchanging randomized initial sequence numbers. It costs one round trip before the client can send data, which is why connection reuse matters for latency.

items.title: TIME_WAIT and who closes first
items.body: The side that actively closes a connection stays in TIME_WAIT for 2*MSL (60 seconds on Linux) so the final ACK can be retransmitted and stray old segments cannot corrupt a new connection with the same 4-tuple. It is normal, not a leak.
items.question: A client opening a new connection per request starts failing with EADDRNOTAVAIL. Why?
items.answer: Thousands of sockets sit in TIME_WAIT, each holding an ephemeral port toward the same destination, until the range is exhausted. Reuse connections with keep-alive or a pool instead of tuning TIME_WAIT away.

items.title: A mysterious 40 ms latency
items.question: A client sends a request as two small writes (header, then body) and waits for a reply. Each call takes an extra 40 ms on Linux. What is happening?
items.answer: Nagle holds the second small write until the first is ACKed, while the server delays its ACK hoping to piggyback on a response, so both wait for the delayed-ACK timer. Coalesce writes into one send, or set TCP_NODELAY for latency-sensitive request/response protocols.

items.title: HTTP/2 stalls on lossy networks
items.question: Your HTTP/2 app multiplexes many streams on one TCP connection and performs worse than HTTP/1.1 on lossy mobile networks. Why?
items.answer: TCP delivers bytes strictly in order, so one lost packet blocks delivery of every stream behind it until it is retransmitted: head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, which does loss recovery per stream, so a loss only stalls the affected stream.

items.title: Why new connections start slow
items.question: Why does a fresh TCP connection on a fast link not transfer at full speed immediately?
items.answer: Congestion control starts with a small congestion window (commonly 10 segments) and roughly doubles it each RTT during slow start until loss or a threshold. Short transfers finish before the window grows, so reusing warm connections and cutting round trips often matters more than bandwidth.

items.title: TCP has no message boundaries
items.body: TCP is a byte stream: one send may arrive split across several reads, and several sends may arrive in one read. Applications must frame messages themselves, with length prefixes or delimiters.
